content:
ASUS ProArt PA27UCGE is a 27-inch 4K monitor that stands out in the highly competitive display market thanks to several unique features. First and foremost is the support for a high refresh rate of up to 160Hz, making it equally adept at smoothly browsing the web, gaming, or video editing. It also comes with an optional monitor hood to reduce ambient light interference, and features a built-in motorized colorimeter for automatic calibration.

We have previously reviewed ASUS's 5K ProArt (review) and 6K ProArt monitors (review), and considered both to be excellent high-value options for Mac users seeking a cost-effective third-party display. How does this 4K ProArt monitor perform? Watch our hands-on video review for the details.

The ASUS ProArt monitor series has traditionally targeted photo editing and video production, and the 27-inch 4K PA27UCGE is no exception. While it cannot deliver the deep, true blacks of OLED technology, I found that this 600-nit IPS panel offers quite respectable contrast and sustained brightness, making it well-suited for use in environments where ambient lighting cannot be fully controlled.

Video: ASUS 4K 160Hz Monitor — Worth Buying?

The PA27UCGE supports variable refresh rates of up to 160Hz at 4K resolution. This not only makes scrolling text smoother, but is also ideal for high-frame-rate video production and gaming. I tested it alongside a 16-inch MacBook Pro with 120Hz ProMotion, and the refresh rates on both displays were perfectly matched, resulting in an excellent user experience. Even when connecting just a single display to the M4 Mac mini, I enjoyed using the 120Hz, 144Hz, or even 160Hz modes.

Although I have always preferred glossy screens over matte designs, the anti-glare, low-reflection "LuxPixel" coating used on this monitor effectively resists reflections while keeping text crisp and sharp, without the text blurring typically associated with standard matte screens. Text sharpness is still somewhat affected, but this is the best matte screen I have encountered — second only to models employing nano-etch technology, such as Apple's matte option.

The PA27UCGE also comes with an optional monitor hood to help block ambient light reflections. I found the process of attaching the hood a bit cumbersome, and its design and build quality feel somewhat clunky, but once installed, it does effectively prevent ambient light from hitting the screen surface.

macOS Scaling

One major drawback of using a 4K display with macOS is the inability to perfectly support native 1:1 HiDPI scaling at 2880×1440 — the setting most users desire on a display of this size. As with all 4K displays, if you set the display to 2560×1440, the system first renders 5120×2880 on a virtual canvas, then uses fractional scaling to downscale to a pixel-doubled 1440p "retina" HiDPI resolution. While the result comes close to a true 5K panel, the imperfect 1:1 scaling causes a slight reduction in text sharpness.

Using the native pixel-doubled resolution of 1920×1080 delivers true 1:1 scaling and exceptionally sharp text, but at the cost of significantly reduced usable screen space. For most people, sacrificing a bit of sharpness in exchange for more space is a perfectly reasonable trade-off, but it is worth noting. I was more sensitive to this issue in my younger years, but as I have grown older, my tolerance has increased and the problem no longer feels as severe.

Calibration Measurements

The monitor's built-in motorized colorimeter, located beneath the logo on the bottom bezel, allows the ProArt 4K to calibrate itself, eliminating the need for external calibration tools or software to achieve more accurate colors. That said, I still prefer using an external device such as the Calibrite Display Pro HL for greater flexibility.

Calibration can be performed via the OSD using the built-in motorized colorimeter, but if you want to view the actual data, you will need to install the ASUS ProArt Calibration tool. The built-in colorimeter is limited by its fixed position, but its key advantage lies in the ability to schedule automatic calibrations when the display is idle. Since the calibration process can easily take 30 minutes or more at any given time, this feature is extremely useful over the long term.

According to the included calibration report, this test unit had an average sRGB Delta-E of 0.78 and an average DCI-P3 Delta-E of 1.12 out of the box — both excellent figures. The Delta-E value measures the difference between the input source color and what the display actually shows; the lower the number, the more accurate the color. In my experience, anything below 2 is considered outstanding.

ASUS states that the PA27UCGE covers 98% of the DCI-P3 color gamut, making it suitable for color grading and video editing in Final Cut Pro or DaVinci Resolve. To verify ASUS's claims, I tested using both the built-in colorimeter and the Calibrite Display Pro HL, paired with Calibrite's Profiler software and ASUS's own ProArt calibration tool.

The measurements showed an average DCI-P3 Delta E of < 1.2, closely matching ASUS's advertised figures. DCI-P3 coverage was equally accurate. When editing and color grading Canon Log 2 footage shot on the Canon R5 Mark II in Final Cut Pro, I found the colors to be largely accurate.

Worth highlighting further, the display panel showed good color and brightness uniformity, with brightness deviations staying within the < 5 threshold across the vast majority of Calibrite Profiler tests. In terms of brightness, the display is rated for a maximum of 600 nits, but during testing it actually peaked at over 700 nits.

Design, Build Quality, and Ergonomics

The ASUS ProArt 4K monitor continues ASUS's traditional design language, and like the previous 5K and 6K ProArt models, its build quality is nothing remarkable. This is not to say that ASUS's quality is poor — it's simply that Apple invests tremendous effort in this area, and its own displays are almost invariably built to a higher standard.

Third-party display makers generally do not compete with Apple on this front. Instead, third-party displays typically offer better value through lower-priced, predominantly plastic housings, which are also easier to mass-produce.

Ultimately, while I would of course love to see ASUS displays adopt unibody aluminum construction with smooth, balanced adjustments, the reality is that virtually no third-party manufacturer is willing to go head-to-head with Apple in this regard. ASUS compensates with greater overall value, higher refresh rates, and a richer selection of I/O options.

Ergonomics

In terms of ergonomics, the ASUS ProArt 4K performs admirably. The display can tilt back 23 degrees or forward 5 degrees, swivel on a pivot 90 degrees to either side, rotate ±30 degrees to either side, and offers 120mm of height adjustment. The overall smoothness and balance of the adjustments fall short of the Apple Studio Display. Apple includes tilt adjustment as standard on the base Studio Display, with the tilt- and height-adjustable stand commanding an additional $200, yet it completely lacks pivot and swivel functionality.

All things considered, the design, build quality, and ergonomics of the ASUS PA27UCGE prioritize practicality over aesthetics. Of course, I would also love to have the clean, logo- and button-free front bezel of the Studio Display, but at $800, this ASUS 4K display undeniably offers tremendous value.

Connectivity

Although Apple upgraded the I/O on the new Studio Display with Thunderbolt 5 connectivity and daisy-chaining, third-party displays like the PA27UCGE offer a richer and more diverse selection of ports.

The USB 3.2 Gen 1 upstream port is the interface most Mac users will use to connect their MacBook or Mac mini. For laptop users, the USB upstream port delivers up to 96W of power — enough to fast-charge a 14-inch MacBook Pro at full speed. The PA27UCGE also features two HDMI 2.1 ports and one DisplayPort 1.4 interface, making it easy to connect a PC, game console, or set-top box such as an Apple TV.

  • Digital Input: 1 x DisplayPort v1.4, 2 x HDMI 2.1, 1 x DisplayPort over USB Type-C
  • USB Ports: 1 x USB 3.2 Gen 1 Upstream Type-C (data only), 1 x USB 3.2 Gen 1 Downstream Type-C, 2 x USB 3.2 Gen 1 Downstream Type-A
  • Audio: Headphone jack, Built-in speakers (2W x 2)

Beyond the built-in USB hub, the monitor also supports auto-KVM functionality, making it convenient to connect two computers simultaneously and share a single mouse and keyboard.

9to5Mac Verdict

The ASUS ProArt PA27UCGE monitor offers exceptional value for its price. It delivers respectable DCI-P3 color support suitable for photo and video editing, and its high refresh rate pairs perfectly with ProMotion-equipped MacBook Pros.

The LuxPixel matte screen resists reflections without overly compromising text clarity. The included monitor hood, while not the most elegant in design, effectively blocks ambient light.

More importantly, this monitor offers a rich array of input interfaces, including two HDMI ports, DisplayPort, and USB-C, along with hub and KVM functionality.

Like most third-party displays on the market, its build quality still trails that of Apple's own displays, but this is a reality faced by virtually all third-party monitors. In compensation, it offers a more comprehensive range of ergonomic adjustments.

ASUS provides a 3-year warranty for ProArt monitors (including the PA27UCGE), which can be extended by an additional 2 years free of charge upon registration, for a total of 5 years of coverage. Considering that most monitors on the market — including Apple's — only offer a 1-year warranty, a 5-year warranty is undeniably very attractive.

It is certainly not flawless, but at $800, this ASUS 4K ProArt monitor far exceeds expectations, and I can wholeheartedly recommend it to video editors or gamers seeking a high-frame-rate, fully featured external display.
